title: Cloud Primitives for Production ML
interviewAnswer: Cloud ML systems are easier to reason about by capability: object storage for data/artifacts, a container registry, scalable compute, managed training/serving, orchestration, observability, identity/networking and a model/metadata layer. AWS, Azure and GCP expose different products for these same architectural needs.
why: Cloud architecture becomes portable when you understand capabilities and trade-offs instead of memorizing one provider’s product catalog.
intuition: Start from the workload: where data lives, how code is packaged, where training/inference runs, how jobs are triggered, how the system is observed and how access is controlled. Only then choose provider-specific services.
deepDive: A production ML stack typically needs durable object storage, a container/image registry, CPU/GPU compute, orchestration, model artifacts/registry, online or batch serving, metrics/logs/traces, IAM/secrets and networking. AWS might use S3/ECR/SageMaker/ECS/EKS/CloudWatch; Azure can combine Blob/ACR/Azure ML/AKS/Monitor; Google Cloud can combine Cloud Storage/Artifact Registry/Vertex AI/GKE or Cloud Run/Cloud Monitoring. These mappings are conceptual, not exact one-to-one equivalents. Managed ML platforms reduce operational burden but may constrain runtime choices or increase platform coupling.
math: Capability map: Data/Artifacts → object storage; Images → container registry; Train/Serve → managed ML or container compute; Orchestration → workflow service; Observe → logs/metrics/traces; Secure → IAM/secrets/network policies.
code:
# Provider-neutral architecture thinking
requirements = [
    "object_storage", "container_registry", "training_compute",
    "serving", "orchestration", "observability", "identity"
]
# Choose services only after latency, scale, GPU, governance and cost requirements are known.
commonMistakes: Treating cloud providers as only different user interfaces.
Choosing a managed ML service before clarifying workload requirements.
Ignoring IAM, networking, data residency and observability when drawing the ML architecture.
followUps: When would you use managed ML serving versus Kubernetes/container compute?
Where should model checkpoints and large artifacts live?
How would you design rollback across providers?
Which parts of the architecture should remain portable?
production: Prefer explicit interfaces between storage, training, serving and monitoring; use least-privilege identities, versioned artifacts, infrastructure-as-code where appropriate, deployment guardrails and cost/latency observability. Portability is a trade-off—use native managed capabilities where they provide clear operational value.
workedExample: An image model can store training data and versioned checkpoints in object storage, keep its inference image in a registry, run GPU inference on a managed endpoint or container platform, expose predictions through an API, and send latency/error/model metrics to the cloud observability stack.
